terms.gloss: a party, a side in politics
evidence: Pollio in Cic. Fam. 10.31.2: nūllīus partis esse
M-O s.v. political party, citing Egger
terms.comment: Usually plural; the singular in nūllīus partis esse, to belong to no party. Rome had sides rather than organised parties; Morgan–Owens gives partēs for a modern party. To join a party, partī sē adjungere (Traupman 179).

evidence: Sall. Jug. 31.15: inter malōs factiō est
terms.comment: Classically mostly a word of reproach: the few and their partisans (Lewis & Short).

evidence: M-O s.v. political party, citing Egger and earlier writers

phrases.latin: cum vērō nōn licēret mihi nūllīus partis esse, quia utrubīque magnōs inimīcōs habēbam
phrases.english: since I could not stay out of both parties, having powerful enemies on each side

phrases.latin: sed haec inter bonōs amīcitia, inter malōs factiō est
phrases.english: but among good men this is friendship; among bad men it is a faction

sources: Lewis & Short: pars · Lewis & Short: factio · Lewis & Short: politicus
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. political party.
Cicero’s letters and Sallust’s Jugurtha checked against the Perseus Latin texts (9 November 2026).
